article.title: OX Security Finds 24 npm Packages Turning Registry Mirrors Into Free Hosting for Fake Cloudflare Phishing Pages
article.summary: OX Security found npm packages hosting fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA pages that redirect visitors once mirrored by UNPKG and npmmirror.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Threat actors are abusing npm and its mirror services to host phishing pages rather than to distribute malware directly, according to research published by [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/) on August 25, 2026. The firm identified 24 npm packages that all contain the same malicious HTML page, which impersonates a Cloudflare CAPTCHA verification screen and redirects visitors to attacker-controlled destinations once the packages are mirrored by services like UNPKG and npmmirror, as also reported by [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/).

## What We Know

- The technique was first spotted in July by security researcher inf0stache, who found a 'china_airlines' npm package using a fake Cloudflare verification page to redirect visitors to a malicious domain, a finding also reported by IntelFusions, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/).
- OX Security, in a report authored by Moshe Siman Tov Bustan and Vitalii Chepurko, said its research "found a total of 24 packages containing the same HTML page, with each package usually reaching between 50-300 weekly downloads before it gets removed," according to [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/).
- Unlike typical npm supply-chain attacks, installing the packages does not infect a developer's machine with malware or infostealers, [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/) reported. Instead, OX Security said the goal is to use "the registry and its mirrors as a safe, validated storage for the malware," according to [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/).
- Each malicious package contains only two files: an index.html page and a package.json file that declares the HTML file as the package's main file, [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/) found after examining one of the packages directly.
- When mirrored by UNPKG, the HTML file becomes directly accessible in a browser through a URL such as https://unpkg.com/ndmxchdjxn2@1.0.0/index.html, according to both [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/) and [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/). Because the page then renders from the legitimate unpkg.com domain rather than attacker infrastructure, it can potentially bypass security software that would otherwise block a malicious site, [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/) reported.
- The malicious HTML impersonates a Cloudflare security verification page and embeds Cloudflare's legitimate Turnstile CAPTCHA service; regardless of whether the verification succeeds, the page runs heavily obfuscated JavaScript that redirects the visitor elsewhere, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/).
- OX Security research team lead Moshe Siman Tov Bustan told BleepingComputer that earlier versions of the packages redirected to microcloud.homes in July and to a typosquatted Microsoft domain, login.microsofte.live, in August, according to [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/). Some of the earliest July redirects ultimately resolved to the legitimate Microsoft Outlook mail login page, outlook.office.com/mail, the outlet reported. BleepingComputer said it tested one of the malicious pages hosted through UNPKG and confirmed it still redirects to the login.microsofte.live domain, though that domain is not currently live.
- Newer packages switched to a different redirect method built on api.keyval.org, a legitimate platform for storing key-value pairs. The code retrieves an encrypted value from the service, decrypts it in the browser, and redirects the visitor to the decrypted URL, letting the attacker change the destination remotely without republishing the npm package, according to [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/) and [BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-abuse-npm-mirrors-to-host-phishing-redirect-pages/). At the time of OX's research, the remotely configured destination redirected to the legitimate ChatGPT website, both outlets reported.
- OX Security recommends treating npm mirror domains — including unpkg, npmmirror, yarn, and tencent — "as potential phishing hosts when not used for downloading package mirrors," adding mirror URLs to phishing detection and URL-reputation pipelines, and checking proxy and DNS logs for direct .html requests to mirror domains, according to [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/).

## What We Don't Know

OX Security has not disclosed who is behind the campaign or their ultimate objective, since the destinations observed so far — a defunct typosquat domain and the legitimate ChatGPT site — do not themselves constitute an active phishing or malware payload. Because the keyval.org-based redirect can be reconfigured remotely at any time, it is not known whether or when the operators will point it toward an active ClickFix page or other malicious destination. BleepingComputer noted that while OX warned the redirect mechanism "could be weaponized to deliver ClickFix or any other phishing domains," the specific npm-hosted HTML it reviewed did not perform a ClickFix attack at the time of testing.

## Analysis

The campaign illustrates a shift in how npm's infrastructure can be abused: rather than using packages to smuggle infostealers or backdoors onto developer machines, the packages here function as disposable, disguised web hosting. Because mirroring services replicate whatever is published to npm — including arbitrary HTML — a package that never needs to be run or imported can still be weaponized simply by existing on a trusted-looking domain. OX Security warned that this persistence problem extends beyond takedowns on the official registry: "since npm packages can live forever in mirrors even after they are removed from the official stores," according to [OX Security](https://www.ox.security/blog/research-clickfix-phishing-npm-packages/). The firm concluded, "Threat actors keep finding and using new and novel techniques not just to deliver malware, but to use legitimate infrastructure to store their payloads and data."
